correctness.rationale: The Gram matrix is a Gauss–Markov innovation covariance and is SPD. Its exact tridiagonal inverse, checked by exact rational reconstruction, becomes irreducible nonnegative after sign conjugation. Raising any adjacent correlation strictly raises both the Perron root of K and that of the sign-conjugated precision, so the spectral condition number strictly rises. The Toeplitz Fourier-symbol interval is strict for nonzero finite trigonometric polynomials. Constant and alternating unit vectors converge to the two symbol edges, yielding sharpness. All n>=2, ell>0, h>0 and target Gamma>1 boundary cases are covered; finite checker examples are not treated as infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The claim is the conjunction of strict gap-by-gap spectral monotonicity, uniqueness of the equal-gap maximizer at every finite size, and the sharp separation-only uniform condition-number constant. Existing inspected sources supply general nonsharp separation estimates or only the equal-gap Toeplitz case. No actual matching theorem was found in mathematical or public literature searches; equivalence to an older Gaussian Markov or total positivity theorem remains a residual priority risk.
residual_risks: A classical Gaussian Markov covariance or total-positivity monograph may have an equivalent strict all-gaps spectral comparison, despite the inspected primary papers and targeted searches.
The exact extremizer does not extend from the 1D exponential kernel to arbitrary radial kernels without a different proof.

value.rationale: The motivating kernel-algorithm work expressly trades center separation against condition-number growth and uses conditioning-controlled center exclusion. An exact extremal point geometry and optimal quantitative separation radius for a canonical Matérn kernel is a natural structural stability result, not a purely renamed classical inequality. It provides an optimal uniform certificate for an arbitrary target condition-number budget and shows that the limiting worst case cannot be attained by any finite sample. It is distinct from mere computation of a known equal-grid eigenvalue table or a general pre-existing nonsharp separation estimate.
